I work in this area - right now, kinda, but not to the extent you're looking for.

It's a fairly straightforward thing to use a visa giftcard, for example, a PO box, and false information to get a test taken. No companies will sell any highly identifiable data about you, but they will sell anonymized data to medical research companies. Ie. Google's Callico is researching longevity and has a deal with Ancestry.com, for example, for large swaths of anonymous data. All US companies are required to comply with valid subpoenas for information which, to my knowledge, has only happened a single time and was used to exonerate someone, not convict them. If you anonymize yourself like I mentioned, it would be fairly hard to track anything to you personally.

My personal recommendation, based on my knowledge of the space, is to use Ancestry.com's DNA service primarily because it is the largest, and the larger the data set, the more accurate the results for where your ancestors are from is. All major services allow you to download your results so that you can use them elsewhere. For health, 23andMe has FDA approval for giving your carrier status of certain diseases, but their test is pretty expensive. Ancestry.com does not have FDA approval yet, but you can download your results from them and upload to somewhere like promethease.com, which uses snpedia to analyze your results, and gives you a bunch of health info.

I'm happy to answer more questions, if you so desire.

Being blunt, you're probably going to have to wait a very, very long time.

The value of services like these is not in the processing of a single person's DNA, but in the network effect of large amounts of people's DNA. Ie. - I can make a reasonable guess based on a few markers about your DNA by running a single test and consulting literature, but if I can get several million people's DNA and do some big data magic on it, I can start to resolve some astounding stuff, both from the medical perspective and from the history/genealogy perspective. Most companies going big in this space are not banking on a business as selling a single product, one-time. They're looking to pull aggregate data out like crazy, and the holy grail is to eventually be able to charge you to tell you things about your history and health that you simply can't get another way. But, that requires crazy amounts of data to pull off.

None of these companies give a crap about your address, phone number, social security number, or any traditionally sensitive crap like that. They are interested in your family tree and family health history.
